article.title: Review: The Wind Cries Freedom: An Oral History of the Next American Revolution
article.author: Detroit DSA
article.content: The cover for The Wind Cries Freedom by Michael Albert By Will Froberg Michael Albert takes you into a parallel universe in which the fictional Revolutionary Participatory Society (RPS) mass movement has grasped the levers of power in the United States, and is now in the process of implementing their participatory vision. Through a series of interviews with RPS organizers, Albert explains the means by which the movement eventually prevailed. Their vision includes an alternative to capitalism called a participatory economy , which the author invented alongside Robin Hahnel back in the 1960’s, and which he has spent his life advocating for. One of the RPS organizers reflects on the direction the movement settled on at their first convention. She describes a participatory economy as being “a system of decentralized, cooperative negotiation between workers’ and consumers’ councils,” in which “resources, workplaces, and the very infrastructure of production were not owned by a few but shared by all.” It is a democratic economy with remuneration for need and effort/sacrifice. Another key component is balanced jobs, which are described in the following passage: “But each worker should be in a position to participate — really participate. That meant restructuring work itself. No more corporate hierarchies where a small class gets the empowering, decision-heavy tasks, and everyone else is left with rote obedience. We called the alternative ‘balanced job complexes.’” I find Albert’s vision difficult to dismiss: it’s comprehensive, rigorous, and strikes a great balance between various values that I believe are highly desirable. One of these values is self-management: that people should have a say in decisions in proportion to the degree they are affected. The RPS program extends well beyond economics. Albert makes very clear how important it is to avoid putting one sphere of relations above any other. He does this by having the organizers also discuss vision and strategy for political, community, and kinship relations — as well as environmental and international relations. This book is very different from Albert’s other works because it does not provide a detailed technical breakdown of either his vision, or even critiques of current systems. Although the interview format can be slightly dry at times, it allows Albert to do what he does best: let his originality flow while communicating ideas simply and, in this case more than in his previous works, evocatively. The book’s coverage is incredibly wide. It covers all the essential facets of what a movement like this would entail: the many tactics and strategies RPS used to win, psychological tendencies they had to contend with, and so much more. Ultimately this is a very human exploration of a movement’s possibilities, struggles, failures, and successes. A surprising bonus was that it is a smooth and easy read. Its ideas often leave you nodding along and asking yourself: “Why didn’t I think of that?” Some of the insights feel like common sense, but only after you encounter them, like when one of the RPS organizers says: “We understood a basic principle that is often lost in political projects: that a less-than-perfect agreement achieved with genuine consensus and mutual trust, real participation, can be far superior to a technically ‘better’ proposal imposed through division or maneuvering.” This book often made me wonder why leftist movements have not already been working like RPS. Perhaps it’s time to! Will Froberg is a DSA member and former editor of The Detroit Socialist. He writes about post-capitalist vision and strategy and works as a data architect for the City of Detroit. Review: The Wind Cries Freedom: An Oral History of the Next American Revolution was originally published in The Detroit Socialist on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
